identity.title: Dullness to percussion with decreased tactile fremitus (focal; conventional vs auscultatory percussion)

technique.how: Patient sitting; percuss the posterior and lateral chest from apex to base, comparing sides at each level, and mark where resonance changes to dull. Then ask the patient to say 'ninety-nine' while palpating the same sites with the ulnar hand edge to grade tactile fremitus. Auscultatory percussion: tap the manubrium while listening over the posterior chest.
technique.prerequisites: Bare skin, patient able to sit or lie lateral, quiet room.

interpretation.positive_finding: Stony dullness with reduced fremitus over a base strongly favors pleural effusion (pooled LR+ 8.7); dullness with increased fremitus and bronchial breathing favors consolidation (LR+ 2.6 for CAP).
interpretation.negative_finding: Normal (non-reduced) tactile fremitus lowers the probability of effusion (LR- 0.21) and may make radiography unnecessary when pretest probability is low.
interpretation.pitfalls: Small effusions (<300-500 mL) are missed; obesity, raised hemidiaphragm, and dense consolidation all produce dullness. Conventional percussion outperforms auscultatory percussion in pooled data.
interpretation.changes_what: Dullness + reduced fremitus: order CXR/POCUS for effusion. Dullness + increased fremitus/egophony: treat as consolidation. Normal fremitus at low pretest probability: may skip imaging.

estimates.population: Adults with respiratory symptoms; 5 prospective studies, N=934
estimates.quote: dullness to conventional percussion was most accurate for diagnosing pleural effusion (summary positive likelihood ratio, 8.7; 95% confidence interval, 2.2-33.8)

estimates.target_condition: Pleural effusion (absence of reduced tactile vocal fremitus)
estimates.population: Adults with respiratory symptoms; 5 prospective studies, N=934
estimates.quote: the absence of reduced tactile vocal fremitus made pleural effusion less likely (negative likelihood ratio, 0.21; 95% confidence interval, 0.12-0.37)

estimates.population: Adults with suspected pneumonia or acute cough; 17 prospective cohorts (9 primary care, 7 ED)

sources.citation: Wong CL, Holroyd-Leduc J, Straus SE. Does this patient have a pleural effusion? JAMA. 2009;301(3):309-317.
Ebell MH, Chupp H, Cai X, Bentivegna M, Kearney M. Accuracy of Signs and Symptoms for the Diagnosis of Community-acquired Pneumonia: A Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2020;27(7):541-553.
Kalantri S, Joshi R, Lokhande T, et al. Accuracy and reliability of physical signs in the diagnosis of pleural effusion. Respir Med. 2007;101(3):431-438.
Metlay JP, Kapoor WN, Fine MJ. Does this patient have community-acquired pneumonia? Diagnosing pneumonia by history and physical examination. JAMA. 1997;278(17):1440-1445.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Not a substitute for imaging when effusion or empyema would change management (e.g., febrile patient with suspected parapneumonic effusion).
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Dullness with fever and hypoxia or with unilateral absent breath sounds and hemodynamic compromise warrants urgent imaging and drainage assessment.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Kalantri 2007 reported kappa 0.84-0.89 for percussion note and vocal fremitus and 0.68-0.78 for auscultatory percussion between two blinded physicians.

extraction_notes: Pooled LRs quoted from Wong 2009 RCE and Ebell 2020 meta-analysis abstracts (full texts not PMC OA, so sensitivity/specificity cells and the auscultatory-percussion row are not visible and left null). Prevalence for Ebell: 10% primary care, 20% ED (reported separately in abstract; not averaged, so left null). Kalantri 2007 cited for reliability only.
